summary:
Incheon has no documented city ordinance, enforcement pattern or incident concerning transgender visitors. Anyone in the city stands under the national framework of South Korea, which does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life and does not restrict access to public facilities by legal status. The criminalising provisions that exist in South Korean law reach only military personnel: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 penalises consensual same-sex conduct among service members with up to two years' imprisonment, a provision the Constitutional Court upheld in 2023, and transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Trans visitors hold a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 22 July 2024 the Seoul High Court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The ruling is final.

The pattern behind that ruling is documented at national level. A 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink to sidestep the question, and 36% went without restroom use altogether. In 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that had barred a transgender student from its restroom.

Legal gender recognition no longer depends on surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not had sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity.

Hostility concentrates at public events, and Incheon is the one South Korean city in this record where a Pride event ended in violence. About 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction. For comparison, at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters.

South Korean national law provides no comprehensive anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity, which is the gap cited by people reporting street-level risk. Healthcare carries an official blind spot flagged from within the state itself: in November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare refused to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

The sharpest documented harm in the national framework concerns Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, a transgender soldier compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.
tangentialFactors:
Outing through public health machinery remains a documented route to harm. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing identified and outed LGBTQ people; doxing and online harassment rose in the aftermath, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

Survey data indicate a discrimination burden that visitors may encounter indirectly through staff and service providers. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, that 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, and that among those recommended it 65.4% reported harm and 94% psychological trauma. A 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the previous year.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 characterises South Korea's overall record on free media and civil society as relatively positive alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people. LGBTI organisations can register, but an NGO that won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 faced government appeal, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Same-sex partnership status does not travel with the visitor: South Korean national law recognises neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt, though a 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights marks the main advance in that area.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition runs through the family register and is available without surgery. Court approval of a registered-sex change is the operative step, and following the Yeongdong ruling of 8 May 2024 the surgical prerequisite no longer applies; guidelines that still mention surgery are reference only. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender people with minor children may have their gender recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent.

Transgender people are excluded from military service, while consensual same-sex conduct between military personnel is criminalised under Military Criminal Act article 92-6 with up to two years' imprisonment. Enforcement has been targeted: in 2017 the military ran what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, criminally charging 32 personnel, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex.

Everyday facilities remain contested for residents as well as visitors. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding on and leaving school early, and researchers called for legal and institutional reform to make school environments safer.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law protecting sexual orientation or gender identity, so employment, housing and service refusals are addressed case by case rather than by statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Incheon-specific ordinance, facility policy or municipal enforcement record on transgender restroom access was found in the source inventory; the restroom rights described rest on national court rulings applied in the city.

The source inventory does not document current conditions at Incheon Pride events after the protest attack, the outcome of the charges organisers filed against pastors, or any disciplinary finding on the alleged police inaction.

Whether Incheon hospitals follow the non-existent national hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients is not sourced; the Ministry of Health and Welfare declined to draft them, and no local compliance data appears in the inventory.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of transgender travellers by South Korean authorities, including passport marker handling at Incheon International Airport, is not covered by any source provided and remains unsourced here.
